name: simdutf8
baseline: Rust std::str::from_utf8 (also compared against simdjson's UTF-8 validator)
workload: UTF-8 validation of valid/invalid ASCII and non-ASCII byte buffers (incl. a 64KiB error case) using criterion benchmarks
claimed_speedup: Up to 23x faster than the std library on valid non-ASCII, up to 4x faster on ASCII (x86-64 Zen2); up to 11x faster than std on non-ASCII, up to 4x on ASCII (Apple M1/aarch64); 'faster than simdjson on almost all inputs'
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.52.0 (x86-64 run), Rust 1.54.0-nightly (aarch64 run); default cargo/criterion release build, exact rustflags not stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 3700 (Zen2), Linux x86-64; Apple M1 (aarch64), macOS
tradeoffs: Requires unsafe SIMD intrinsics internally; 'basic' API omits error position (use 'compat' API for that, at a small perf cost); runtime CPU-feature dispatch adds a small branch.
caveats: Benchmark numbers are from 2021 (Rust 1.52/1.54); not benchmarked directly against simdutf (C++) or ICU, only against Rust's own std library and simdjson's validator.

name: ada-url/idna
workload: IDNA to_ascii domain-name Unicode processing (UTS #46), Google Benchmark 'to_ascii' tool on Apple M1 Max
claimed_speedup: 1504 ns/op, 48.5 M/s, 3.99 M url/s (Ada) vs 1898 ns/op, 38.5 M/s, 3.16 M url/s (ICU) -- about 1.26x faster (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: LLVM 14 (clang), C++20; exact optimization flags beyond the provided CMake benchmark build are not itemized
stars_or_usage: 69 stars; used by Node.js and referenced in a ClickHouse PR (per README)
tradeoffs: C++20 required; scope is limited to IDNA to_ascii/to_unicode (domain-name encoding), not general-purpose UTF-8 validation or transcoding.
caveats: Category fit is imperfect: this is IDNA/domain-name Unicode processing (TR46), not raw UTF-8 validate/transcode. Only one micro-benchmark result is shown in the README; build flags are not fully itemized beyond the compiler version.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than ICU"

name: Boost.Text (tzlaine/text)
workload: UTF-8<->UTF-16/UTF-32 transcoding and NFC normalization of ~0.5MB Wikipedia text (European and non-European languages, NFC-input and NFD-input) using Google Benchmark
claimed_speedup: '[Text] is factors faster than ICU's UTF-8 code path, and a bit faster than ICU's much faster UTF-16 code path' for NFC-normalizing NFC-input European text; 'In every case, [Text] is faster than the UTF-8 ICU code path.' (exact numbers exist only as SVG bar charts, not as text/tables)
compiler_and_flags: GCC (version unspecified) on Linux; optimization flags not stated
tradeoffs: Header-heavy Boost-style API; back-inserter-based usage is much slower, so gains are only realized through the pointer-to-pointer bulk transcoding APIs.
caveats: No CPU model or compiler flags are stated, and the only numeric results are embedded in SVG bar-chart images (not extractable as text), so this is capped at Tier C. The author's own doc says results are worse than ICU for non-European text and for NFD-starting input. No commits since Jan 2024.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than ICU" (doc/performance.qbk)

name: xutf
workload: UTF-8/UTF-16/UTF-32 transcoding, grapheme iteration, width/truncation and string equality on ~1MiB ascii/cjk/emoji corpora; criterion benchmarks, best-of-7, on an Apple M4 Max and a Xeon x86-64 host
claimed_speedup: 'beats simdutf across nearly the entire grid, ASCII included, roughly 1.5-2x ahead on typical text, and 3-10x ahead on emoji-heavy input'; e.g. UTF-32->UTF-8 emoji-4b: 18.0 GB/s (xutf) vs 4.6 GB/s (simdutf) on Apple M4 Max; UTF-8->UTF-16 cjk-3b: 8.1 GB/s (xutf) vs 6.7 GB/s (simdutf) on Xeon (+20.9%)
compiler_and_flags: rustc via `cargo bench`, RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" (per scripts/bench_hosts.sh)
hardware: Apple M4 Max; a second host labeled only 'Xeon x86-64' (exact CPU model not given)
tradeoffs: Rust-only (no_std, zero dependencies) so not directly callable from C++ without FFI; decoding is designed to never fail (lossy on malformed input), which changes error-handling semantics versus strict validators like simdutf; younger and far less battle-tested than simdutf.
caveats: One of the two benchmark hosts ('Xeon x86-64') lacks an exact CPU model, weakening reproducibility. Very young/low-star project (10 stars). Author explicitly excludes simdutf's validation-skipping convert_valid_* fast path from the comparison as 'a different question', so this compares against simdutf's full validating path only.

name: Parabix (bitstream UTF-16 validation kernel)
workload: UTF-16 validation of 128/256MiB multilingual text corpora (cjk, emoji-heavy, ascii-heavy, european-accented, mixed-multilingual, south-asian), single-threaded, median of 7 runs with 2 warmups
claimed_speedup: Adjusted (overhead-subtracted) throughput on Apple M1: Parabix SIMD ~5100-5200 MiB/s vs simdutf ~1880-2600 MiB/s depending on dataset (roughly 2x-2.7x); project's own summary states 'Parabix beats simdutf by ~2.3-2.5x (adjusted) on both hosts'
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101) driving an LLVM 16.0.6 JIT backend for Parabix codegen, build_type=Release (per results/apple_arm64_toolchain.md); x86-64 leg used simdutf's SSE4.2 'westmere' path under QEMU
hardware: Apple M1, 8 GiB RAM (primary, native); a CSIL x86-64 host run inside a QEMU guest (secondary, explicitly flagged by the benchmark authors as 'not Ice Lake')
tradeoffs: Parabix requires an LLVM JIT toolchain at build/run time (heavier dependency, ~0.019s fixed per-process overhead vs simdutf's ~0.002s); this benchmark validates UTF-16, not UTF-8; it is a research/academic codebase without a stable packaged API.
caveats: The GitHub repo is an 'Automated Mirror' last pushed 2021-08-12; canonical development happens off-GitHub at SFU's cs-git-research server and may be more current than this mirror. No OSI license file is present in the mirror (only a bundled LLVM license), hence usability='reference'. The benchmark itself was run and published by an unrelated, unlicensed, 0-star student course-project repo (dakshkashyap/cmpt479-project-group8), not by Parabix's own maintainers or a peer-reviewed paper -- methodology is fully public and instrumented, but the source is not notable/independent in the usual sense. The x86-64 leg ran inside a QEMU guest, which the benchmark authors themselves say is not representative of native hardware; the Apple M1 leg is the more trustworthy one. Category fit: this is UTF-16 validation, adjacent to but not identical to 'UTF-8'.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than ICU4X" / "beats" simdutf -> dakshkashyap/cmpt479-project-group8 docs/PROJECT_PLAN.md

name: unicode-transforms
baseline: ICU (ICU4C 65.1, via the text-icu Haskell binding)
workload: Unicode NFC/NFKC/NFD/NFKD normalization of per-language text files (Korean, Vietnamese, Deutsch, English, Devanagari, Japanese, AllChars), milliseconds per file
claimed_speedup: Up to +376.87% faster (NFKD/Korean: 7.78ms vs ICU 37.10ms); results are mixed, not uniform -- e.g. NFC/Japanese is -292.04% (11.90ms vs ICU 3.04ms) and NFKC/AllChars is -50.51%, i.e. ICU wins those cases
tradeoffs: Haskell-only API (Data.Text.Normalize), not usable from C/C++ directly; performance varies heavily by script and normalization form.
caveats: No CPU model, GHC version, or compiler flags are stated in the README, so this is capped at Tier C despite a clear first-party numeric table. Results are genuinely mixed: ICU is faster for Japanese text and for the combined 'AllChars' NFC/NFKC cases. Benchmark is versioned against unicode-transforms v0.3.7, an older release; no date given for when it was run.
